body:
Byungju Kim, Chairman of MBK Partners, who previously testified at a recent National Assembly audit that he did not participate in the operation of Homeplus, was found to have had an obligation under the articles of association of certain blind funds used for the acquisition of Homeplus to be actively involved in managing portfolio companies. He was also obligated to maintain entitlement to performance fees. While these obligations may not require hands-on daily management of Homeplus, some have argued that he could nevertheless be held responsible for major decisions. In response, MBK Partners explained that these are standard duties of good faith for blind funds and are not requirements to participate in the day-to-day operation of individual companies.

According to the articles of association for "MBK Partners Fund III-2," submitted by the office of Park Sanghyuk, a member of the National Assembly's Political Affairs Committee, to the Financial Supervisory Service on October 7, Kim is classified as "key personnel." Key personnel are core management staff within the General Partner (GP) of the fund. The articles list a total of six key personnel: Chairman Kim; Vice-Chairmen Yoon Jongha, Bu Jaehoon, and Kim Kwangil; and two overseas executives, Kong Te Chien and Kung Kuo Chan, who were partners at the time.

Key personnel are subject to obligations related to work hours and diligence according to the articles of association. In particular, there is a duty to be involved in the management of portfolio companies. The articles state that "at least five key personnel shall be actively involved in the management of the company and portfolio companies, regardless of whether this is before or after the end of the capital commitment period." Since the minimum is five, there is a possibility that Kim could be excluded from this requirement, as the five-person condition could still be met without him. However, both Kong Te Chien and Kung Kuo Chan, as overseas partners, were managing investments in Greater China and were likely based overseas. Given their overseas roles, it is highly unlikely they were involved in running domestic companies acquired through the fund. If both Kim and the two foreign partners were excluded, this would violate the articles of association. Consequently, some argue it would be more reasonable to include Chairman Kim as one of the five and add only one overseas partner.

Byungju Kim, Chairman of MBK Partners, appears as a witness at the National Assembly's Political Affairs Committee audit on the Fair Trade Commission, Personal Information Protection Commission, and others held on the 14th. 2025.10.14 Photo by Hyunmin Kim

It was also revealed that Chairman Kim is entitled to receive performance fees. The articles stipulate that "key personnel must retain the right to receive, directly or indirectly, at least 50% of the performance fees." Performance fees are paid on returns that exceed the agreed-upon hurdle rate, and thus are profits that can be earned by increasing a company's value. If key personnel violate either the requirement to be involved in portfolio company management or the entitlement to performance fees, there are penalties—such as suspension of the commitment period or a reduction in the management fees paid on undrawn commitments.

Fund III-2, together with Fund III, are blind funds used by MBK for acquisitions such as Homeplus. A blind fund raises capital to invest in assets that are not predetermined at the time of fundraising. Unlike Fund III, only Fund III-2's articles contain explicit language regarding the duties of operational involvement and performance fee allocation.

MBK Partners responded that such language is a standard clause in blind fund agreements, meant to ensure a duty of good faith and exclusivity, rather than a duty to manage individual companies. MBK stated, "The obligations regarding work hours and diligence are standard duties of exclusivity for blind funds. It means key personnel are expected to devote themselves with good faith to the GP’s affairs, not to engage in other work outside the scope of the blind fund and its portfolio companies." MBK further emphasized that, given blind funds invest in over ten companies, Fund III's equity stake in the Homeplus acquisition was only KRW 500 billion. "More than KRW 2 trillion in main funding was raised through joint investments or separate project funds, such as redeemable convertible preferred shares (RCPS) invested in by the National Pension Service," the company added.

Since the blind fund in question targets Asia as a whole, foreign partners were also included as key personnel, and MBK said that how roles are divided among key personnel for matters related to the fund and investment targets is an internal matter for the GP. Regarding Kim's previous parliamentary testimony, the company explained that his answer meant he did not participate in the day-to-day management of individual companies, including Homeplus.

MBK maintains there are similar obligations in the Fund III articles as well. Both Fund III and Fund III-2 are domestic private equity funds dedicated to investments in Korea, but MBK argues they are functionally the same, and that the overall fund articles drafted with overseas limited partners (LPs) include these obligations, with differences only arising during the local registration process.

However, some point out that submitting articles of association with differing terms for funds with the same purpose to the Financial Supervisory Service during the domestic private equity fund registration process could be problematic. According to Article 249-10 of the Financial Investment Services and Capital Markets Act, an establishment report must be submitted when creating an institutional private equity fund, and the Presidential Decree requires the articles of association to be attached. Furthermore, under Article 446, Item 43, of the same law, those failing to report or making false reports can face up to one year of imprisonment or a fine of up to KRW 30 million.

Some interpret the obligation as requiring Chairman Kim to be involved in major decisions pertaining to portfolio companies, even if he did not engage in the everyday management of Homeplus. On October 14 of last year, in response to Park's question as to whether he was involved in Homeplus's decision-making, Kim answered, "We are not a conglomerate, nor am I a controlling shareholder. We are a PEF operator. Each of our 13 partners is responsible for their respective domain. My domain is fundraising and managing investments made with the raised money." On other matters, such as guarantees for supplier payments, commercial paper redemption, and corporate rehabilitation processes, he stated he had no authority and was not involved.

Industry experts generally view the typical obligations written into blind fund articles as declaratory, encouraging key personnel to "act with diligence," rather than to actively intervene in day-to-day management. However, some argue that, given the role of private equity operators, it is natural for key personnel to participate in overseeing portfolio companies. It has also been suggested that the use of differing language in the articles is partly due to early industry practices of copying precedent fund articles and because LPs sometimes require specific clauses to be included.

Assemblyman Park stated, "Although Chairman Kim testified during last year’s parliamentary audit that decision-making relating to Homeplus was outside his authority, the fund articles for the acquisition of Homeplus designate him as key personnel, obligating him to be actively involved in the management of portfolio companies. Since his parliamentary testimony and the fund articles are inconsistent, a thorough investigation is necessary to determine Chairman Kim's level of involvement in Homeplus management."
